Smart Swipes

By: Floris Kotze | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Smart Swipe: Making Your Rand Go Further

Unique Selling Point:
The unique selling point is that it uncovers the psychology and real impact of loyalty programs in South Africa—not as a promotional piece, nor as a hard investigation, but as a relatable, eye-opening look at how these programs shape our spending habits in tough economic times.

Summary:
This isn’t a generic loyalty program story—it’s about how South Africans, actively use and believe in these programs to stretch their money.

Further information:
Loyalty Programs as a Modern Currency: The idea that points, cashback, and discounts have become a form of financial survival in SA’s current economy—people actively chase rewards to stretch their rands.
The Data Trade-Off: Consumers feel like they’re winning, but loyalty programs are also a massive business built on our data—and most of us don’t even think about it.
The hook? South Africans love loyalty programs—but are they really helping us save, or are we just playing the game exactly as companies planned?

Script:


Smart Swipes | 6671 Script
Opening – Setting the Scene
(Montage of people swiping loyalty cards, scanning QR codes, and using apps at checkout. Fast cuts, upbeat energy.)
Upsounds from YouTube:
Businesses today are using all kinds of techniques in order to keep customers. One of these techniques is loyalty points.
The loyalty industry is not child’s play, it is a proper industry.
The rewards program is a strong American concept. It's believed the concept will continue to grow here at home, becoming more diverse and sophisticated.

PTC – Claire:
Your wallet, your phone, your morning coffee, your groceries.
Every time you shop, fill up or book a flight, chances are you're earning points, getting cash back or unlocking a discount.

VO1:
But in return, we share our data, our shopping habits, even our daily routines. So, are we really winning? And is it worth it?

PTC – Claire
Today, we speak to someone who literally wrote the book on loyalty rewards.

VO2:
Amanda Cromhout knows loyalty programs inside out. She’s spent over 30 years in the industry, working with big brands like British Airways and Woolworths. Now, she runs Truth, a company that helps businesses build better rewards programs.

Claire:
When did the uptake of loyalty rewards programs start in South Africa?
Amanda Cromhout
Programs that we've heard about and are still going strong have been around for three decades. Clicks, for example, this year is celebrating its 30th year of clubcard. I mean, that's a phenomenal long time.

Claire:
So how would you define a loyalty program? What is it?

A good loyalty program is good for the consumer and it makes the whole brand experience more with that brand better, whether it's through points and prizes and experiences and service enhancement because you're part of that loyalty program.
We're in an era without doubt of big data, data, as they say, is the new oil of the world. And a good loyalty program with permission from the consumer collects data. And behind the scenes with permission now, the legislation's really good at making sure there's permission, but a good loyalty program allows the brand to truly understand their customers. And ideally, one hopes that that brand then gives a much enhanced customer experience, better products, better discounts, more relevance, in terms of communication and offers and rewards. So, the customer walks away with a much better experience.

PTC
Every tap, swipe or scan gives companies valuable information about how we shop, where we shop and when we shop. But do we actually care?

Wendy Knowler
Interestingly, a lot of South Africans are quite protective of their personal information and outraged if they deem it to be used in a way that they didn't authorize. When it comes to loyalty programs, often to get on a higher tier, they'll want you to do an extra survey or provide extra information about yourself. And mostly consumers are happy to do that.

Upsound Wendy
Here's something that many cell phone owners don't realize…

VO3:
Consumer journalist Wendy Noller has been following South Africa's loyalty trends for years. She says loyalty programs have evolved dramatically, becoming a bigger part of everyday financial advice.

Wendy Knowler
These loyalty programs are definitely playing a more and more significant role in South Africans' lives. What I've seen happen in the last year or two, when organisations are giving advice to consumers, they will say investigate the loyalty programs that you're on and in terms of getting the most out of them.

Amanda Cromhout
So the most basic is a points-based program. You walk into a store and you swipe your loyalty card or loyalty app and you get points or cash back behind the scenes and that accumulates. You can use the money as cash back. Other programs, you walk into the store and it's immediately the benefits are there for you, whether it's discount because of this or three for two offers because you're part of the loyalty program. But in the airline industry, for example, the higher the tier, you get lounge access, you get priority boarding. So it's more of a service enhancement as well as the financial return.

VO4:
One of the biggest loyalty programs in South Africa is ShopRite Checkers Xtra Savings. A jaw-dropping 29.4 million people swipe their cards in store. That's almost four times the number of people who paid tax last year.(...) Safe to say, ShopRite Checkers probably knows more about South Africans' behavior than SARS does!

VO5:
BUT, not all rewards are about saving money. While data drives loyalty programs everywhere, here, it’s not about what you buy, but showing up.

Kia Abbott: Virgin Active Group Chief of Customer Value
In our space, we don't have any transactional data. We're not trying to incentivise another basket, a bigger basket. So it's really all about participation and we want to reward participation.

VO6:
Virgin Active’s Group Chief of Customer Value, Kia Abbot, has a unique challenge—keeping members motivated.

Kia Abbott: Virgin Active Group Chief of Customer Value
We want to retain our members for life, you know, we're a subscription business. People join on a 12-month subscription.(...) And we know that people who use our facilities more often are achieving their goals are much more likely to renew that membership at the end of the year. And the data that we collect really tries to predict how well somebody is staying on track to meet their goals, if there's a sudden drop. You know, maybe you've had a personal event. Maybe something's changed in your life and you suddenly are not coming back to the gym. And then we can reach out and say, what can we do to support you in the right way to make sure that you can come back and get re-engaged?



VO7:
From gyms to retail, South Africans are all in on loyalty programs— with over 150 to choose from. More than 80% of us are signed up and actively using an average of 10 programmes! Safe to say, we LOVE our rewards!

Voxie 1
We know the times today, you know, I mean, we obviously want to save a buck. And then also with the loyalty programs, you get cash back as well, especially with dust shims. So whenever you buy at Dischem, whatever the amount is, you get a certain amount back as well. And you can accumulate that amount in buy, close to places at the end of the year.
Voxie 2
If I come to the place where I have that loyalty card, then I will look for, you know,
those specials and use it accordingly.
Claire: So do you think it really makes a difference to your household budget to have those loyalty?
Voxie 2: Yeah, for sure.

Amanda Cromhout
There's so many programs that have successful tiered programs, but you have to accept as a consumer whether you're going to make it or not. So you have to make some choices. So if you want to play in all the programs equally, you're never going to make any one of them really successful for you.

VO8:
And when it comes to playing the loyalty game right, we found a self-confessed vitality guru, someone who proves that if you know the rules, the rewards can be seriously worth it.

Matthew Carr
My name is Matthew Carr, and I'm not a part of any other loyalty program, but I am a discovery super user.

Matthew Upsound:
I spent obviously spent 1,500 rewards the week before.



VO9:
By tracking his fitness, driving carefully and shopping smart, he's turning everyday choices into big savings, free coffees, fuel discounts, flight perks, even life insurance benefits.


Claire:
Explain to me how you've made Discovery work for you.
Matthew Carr
Discovery has all of my products. The program works that the more integrated you are, the wider the benefit range. You know, if you think about your car insurance, I drive very carefully. I give you a reward from discovery because I drive carefully. If I think about the food that I eat to nourish my body, I make sure that I, well, I was doing that in any way, but when I've discovered that you're rewarded for eating that way, it made sense to do that because then I'm being rewarded financially. My gym fees should be a thousand a month, that 250 a month, that 230 a month. And I get 1800 back in my fuel spend. Every month I'm getting from the food part, at least R 2500 with the miles a month. I think if I had to get into real specifics about numbers and yeah…
Claire:
Are we talking tens of thousands of rands?
Matthew Carr:
Hundreds of thousands.
Claire:
Are you talking hundreds of thousands of rands?
I listen, I want the hundreds of thousands of rands back a year. It is almost built around certain types of people who are living that way, any way.

VO10
Earning these kinds of rewards every year takes focus and dedication. Matthew's advice, pick a program that fits your lifestyle, not the other way around.

Wendy Knowler
A lot of us have a lot going on in our lives and I'm one of those people that doesn't look for extra ways to add admin to my life. But I can say it's certainly worthwhile making loyalty programs part of your decision. They potentially can give you much financial relief if you use them properly.
Amanda Cromhout
South Africans need loyalty programs and that's the rising cost of living.
But if you're sitting on the fence between two competing brands and study both, not, it doesn't need a PhD to study the loyalty program, just have a look and go, if I was to spend R100 with both, what would I get back?
If you can't pick that up and understand it is the brand is failing, not you.

VO:11
Loyalty programs aren’t going anywhere—in fact, it is growing. Signing up is your choice, but every time you swipe or scan, your data is part of the deal. The good news? South Africa’s POPI Act is there to protect us, ensuring companies handle our data responsibly. But regardless of the legislation, it seems we’ve already decided—the swipe IS worth it!
Final Montage – Fast cuts of swipes, scans, rewards apps, people shopping.

Promo 1:
VO:
Loyalty programs promise big rewards, but do they really help us save, or do they just make us spend more?
Upsound – Wendy Knowler:
"The return per spend is also a competitive thing between the various retailers who offer loyalty programs, and so that’s becoming better for consumers. But it can also be overwhelming—figuring out where the best value is and which programs work best for your needs."
VO:
We break it all down and show you how to make your loyalty points work for you!

Promo 2:
VO:
We all love a good deal, but when it comes to loyalty rewards, who’s really coming out on top?
Upsound – Wendy Knowler:
"Loyalty programs can save you money—but only if you know how to work them!"
VO:
Are they designed to help us… or to make us spend more?

Promo 3:
VO:
Loyalty cards, bonus points, surprise discounts—it all sounds great, right? But behind every swipe, there’s data…
Upsound – Amanda Cromhout:
"Brands invest in loyalty programs to keep you coming back—and the data they collect is gold!"
VO:
So, are these rewards really worth it?


Loyalty programmes offer big rewards, cashback, discounts and perks.(...) But in return, we share our data, our shopping habits, even our daily routines.(...) So, are we really winning? And is it worth it?
